title: The olive tree (Romans 11)
hookLine: Gentiles are grafted into Israel's olive tree; God's gifts are irrevocable

lines: A NEW BRANCH FITTED INTO THE WOUND.
PAUL SAYS IT WITH A TREE.
cards: Some olive trees on the hillsides of the Holy Land are centuries old: trunks twisted like rope, still bearing fruit. A farmer who wants a better tree doesn't plant a new one.
He cuts a branch, fits a new one into the wound, binds it, and waits. That's grafting. The new branch lives on the old root's water and strength.
Paul, still wrestling with yesterday's question, says one more thing about his people and the new Gentile believers in Rome, with a tree.

teach.h: HATH GOD CAST AWAY HIS PEOPLE?
teach.b: Chapter eleven opens with a question, in the King James Bible: "I say then, Hath God cast away his people? God forbid." His answer is no, and he's his own proof: I'm an Israelite too, he says. Then the tree.
Israel is a cultivated olive tree, rooted in the promises to Abraham. Some of its natural branches, he says, have been broken off.
And Gentile believers, people from the nations, are like shoots from a wild olive, grafted in among the branches, drawing life from the root. Here's the surprise: that's backward.
Farmers usually graft a good branch onto a wild root, not a wild branch onto a good one.
Paul seems to know it; he calls it contrary to nature. The Gentiles got in by a move no farmer would make.

Then he turns to the newcomers in Rome, who may have been getting proud: "Boast not against the branches. But if thou boast, thou bearest not the root, but the root thee." You don't hold up the tree. The tree holds you.

teach.h: THE GIFTS OF GOD ARE NOT TAKEN BACK.
teach.b: Then a line many Christians and Jews in conversation today treasure: "For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance." Without repentance means God doesn't take them back.

teach.h: THOU BEAREST NOT THE ROOT, BUT THE ROOT THEE.
teach.b: Paul even hopes the broken branches will be grafted in again, and says that all Israel shall be saved, though Christians differ on what he meant.
Then, having thought as hard as he can, Paul stops thinking and starts praising: "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God!"
At the edge of his argument, he doesn't pretend to have it all figured out. He bows.

how: Many Christians speak of the Jewish roots of their faith, and some churches mark this with study of the Hebrew Scriptures, Jewish-Christian dialogue, and reflection on Romans 11 during Holocaust remembrance.

practice: Think about where your own faith, your questions, or your sense of right and wrong came from: a grandmother who prayed, a teacher, a congregation, a tradition much older than you that someone carried to you across centuries.
Picture those roots under you like the old olive tree's; you didn't grow them, and they're holding you. Name one, and give thanks; if you pray, thank God for them by name.
